script: R-CHOP is a combination of five medicines used to treat certain lymphomas, which are cancers of the lymph system. Its name comes from the first letter of each drug: Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin—also known as Hydroxydaunorubicin—vincristine, which is also called Oncovin, and Prednisone. Four of these medicines are given by IV on day 1 of each treatment cycle. Prednisone, however, is a pill you'll take at home for 5 days. While treatment cycles are most often 21 days long, some treatment plans use 14-day, or 'dose-dense,' cycles. These shorter cycles are given with growth-factor support. A typical course involves 6 cycles, usually given 3 weeks apart, adding up to about 18 weeks in total.

script: Here's roughly what one 3-week cycle feels like: On Day 1, your infusion day, you'll spend several hours at the infusion center. The first time you receive rituximab, it's given slowly over a few hours so we can watch for any reactions. The other three IV drugs are faster. You'll likely get anti-nausea and anti-allergy medicine beforehand. Most people feel okay, maybe a little tired, for the rest of that day. For Days 2 through 5, you'll continue taking prednisone. Remember to take it with food and not at night, as it can keep you awake. Some people notice a temporary 'boost' of energy or feel restless during this time, followed by a dip once they stop taking it. Around days 7 to 10, often called the 'nadir,' your white blood cell count is typically at its lowest. This is why infection precautions are most important during this specific window of time. For Days 11 through 21, most people gradually start to feel more like themselves as their blood counts recover, leading up to the next cycle. You should also know that if hair loss happens, it usually starts within about 3 weeks of your first infusion. And don't be alarmed if your urine is red or orange on the day of and day after your infusion; that's just the color of the doxorubicin drug, not blood.

script: You might find it helpful to plan for a lighter workload or some time off around your infusion day and for a few days afterward. Your energy often picks back up toward the end of your cycle. How much time you need can vary a lot by person and job, so it's reasonable to plan for the lighter end until you know how your body responds. Light activity, like short walks, usually helps with fatigue, constipation, and your mood more than staying in bed. Of course, always rest when you need to. Just remember to avoid new, intense exercise or contact sports during those low blood count windows, which are typically around days 7 to 10, because of the risk of bruising or infection. Driving is generally safe for you, as long as you're not feeling dizzy, overly fatigued, or taking a new medicine that might make you sleepy. Some anti-nausea drugs, for instance, can cause drowsiness. If you're ever in doubt, it's best not to drive that day. Physical intimacy is generally safe for you. For information about protecting your partner, you'll want to refer to the 'fertility and intimacy' section. Planning your chores and appointments for the second half of each cycle, when your energy is more likely to return, can be really helpful. Also, keeping a simple symptom log can assist both you and your care team in spotting any patterns from one cycle to the next.

script: Here, we'll talk about the common effects most people notice at some point during R-CHOP treatment. Some of these you can manage with simple self-care, while others are worth a call to your care team. For each one, we'll tell you what to do. This treatment temporarily lowers your infection-fighting white blood cells, especially around days 7–10. It's very important to know that a fever is a medical emergency at any point in your treatment, not a routine call to your team. Please check the emergency section for the exact temperature threshold and what steps to take. To help prevent issues, wash your hands often and try to avoid crowds and anyone who is sick. Your team might also give you a growth-factor injection to help your white blood cell counts recover faster. You should call your team if you experience chills without a fever, a sore throat, a cough, painful urination, unusual tiredness, or any red, swollen, or painful skin area. You might notice that you bruise or bleed more easily than usual because your platelet count might be lower. To help manage this, use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor. Avoid NSAIDs, like ibuprofen, unless your team tells you it's okay, and always blow your nose gently. Call your team if you have a nosebleed that won't stop after 5 minutes of pressure, a cut that keeps bleeding, significant gum bleeding, blood in your urine or stool, or a severe headache. You may feel unusually tired, weak, or look pale, which happens because of a temporary drop in your red blood cells. To help with this, pace your activities, make sure to prioritize sleep, and avoid driving or operating heavy machinery when you're feeling very tired. Call your team if you experience shortness of breath, dizziness, a fast or irregular heartbeat, or if your fatigue is so severe that it keeps you from your basic daily activities and doesn't improve with rest at all. Nausea is a common side effect, but it's usually well-controlled with the medicine your team gives you before and after your infusion. A key tip for self-care is to take your anti-nausea medicine on schedule, even if you feel fine, because it works much better as prevention than as treatment. Also, try eating small, bland, and frequent meals. You should call your team if you're vomiting for more than 24 hours, can't keep fluids down, show signs of dehydration, or see blood or a coffee-ground appearance in your vomit. The treatment can irritate the lining of your mouth, sometimes causing sores. To care for this, rinse your mouth with a mild salt and baking-soda mixture after meals and at bedtime. Use a soft toothbrush and try to avoid acidic, spicy, or rough foods. Call your team if you have pain or mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink. Changes in your bowel habits, either diarrhea or constipation, are common. These can be caused by the chemotherapy itself, the steroid you're taking, or even your anti-nausea medicine. If you have diarrhea, make sure to hydrate well and stick to low-fiber bland foods. For constipation, also hydrate, try some gentle activity, and include fiber if you can tolerate it. You should call your team if you have 4 or more bowel movements above your normal in 24 hours, if you experience bloody diarrhea, or if your constipation lasts for 3 or more days. The vincristine medication can cause tingling, numbness, or pain, most often in your hands or feet. This is called peripheral neuropathy, and reporting it early matters so your team can help manage it. For self-care, check your feet daily for any injuries you might not feel, and wear well-fitting shoes. Call your team if you notice pins-and-needles sensations or a burning feeling that is new or getting worse, if you have trouble moving your arms or legs, or if you experience balance problems. Hair loss is common with this regimen, usually starting within a few weeks of your first infusion. Your hair typically grows back after treatment ends, though its texture and color might be a bit different at first. You might consider getting a short haircut beforehand, and using scarves, hats, or wigs can be helpful. Remember to protect your scalp from the sun. The cyclophosphamide medication can irritate your bladder. Staying well-hydrated around infusion days is the main prevention, so make sure to drink plenty of water, especially on days 1 through 3 of each cycle. It’s expected to see red or orange urine on the day of and the day after your infusion. However, call your team if your urine is still discolored after 2 days, if you see clots, or if it burns when you urinate. The prednisone you take can cause mood swings, irritability, trouble sleeping, and an increased appetite or blood sugar while you're taking it, which is usually on days 1 through 5 of each cycle. Some people also notice a "crash"—like low energy or a low mood—for a day or two after they stop taking it each cycle, as their body adjusts back down. To help with these effects, take your prednisone in the morning with food, not at night. Let people close to you know that these changes can happen so they aren't mistaken for something else. Gentle activity and a consistent sleep routine can also be helpful. If you have diabetes or are at risk, monitor your blood sugar more closely during these days, following your team's guidance. Call your team if your mood changes feel severe, if you have thoughts of self-harm, or if your symptoms don't ease up once you're a few days past the taper.

However, call your team if your urine is still discolored after two days, if you see clots, or if it burns when you urinate. The prednisone you take can cause mood swings, irritability, trouble sleeping, and an increased appetite or blood sugar while you're taking it, which is usually on days one through five of each cycle. Some people also notice a crash, like low energy or a low mood, for a day or two after they stop taking it each cycle, as their body adjusts back down. To help with these effects, take your prednisone in the morning with food, not at night. Let people close to you know that these changes can happen so they aren't mistaken for something else. Gentle activity and a consistent sleep routine can also be helpful. If you have diabetes or are at risk, monitor your blood sugar more closely during these days, following your team's guidance. Call your team if your mood changes feel severe, if you have thoughts of self-harm, or if your symptoms don't ease up once you're a few days past the taper.

script: Most people never experience these issues. We're listing them so you'll know exactly what to do quickly if they happen. A fever during your low-blood-cell window, which is roughly days 7 to 10 after treatment, is a medical emergency. This happens when your infection-fighting white blood cells are low, and it's called neutropenic fever. You'll need to call your care team immediately, day or night, if you have a temperature of 100.4°F (38.0°C) or higher for an hour, or a single reading of 101°F (38.3°C) or higher. Don't wait for office hours or to see if it comes down. This is different from a fever during an infusion reaction, which the infusion team is already watching for. It's important to treat any fever at this threshold as an emergency at any point in your treatment, not just during this specific window, because you have no way to know your counts on a given day. An infusion reaction can happen during or right after your treatment. Signs include chills or shaking, itching or a rash, trouble breathing or wheezing, tongue swelling, dizziness or faintness, fever, or pain in your back or neck. If this happens during treatment, tell the infusion team immediately. You should also be aware of signs of a serious allergic or skin reaction. These include painful mouth or skin sores, blistering, peeling skin, or a widespread rash. Because doxorubicin can affect the heart, especially at higher lifetime doses, watch for heart symptoms like swelling in your belly, legs, hands, or feet, shortness of breath, new or worsening chest pain or pressure, or a rapid weight gain of 5+ lbs in a day. The risk of heart problems is low, but it climbs steeply if you've received doxorubicin before, even for a prior cancer, which is why disclosing any previous treatment is very important. Signs of a serious brain or nerve problem include confusion, sudden loss of balance, trouble walking or talking, one-sided weakness, or new vision problems. Finally, watch for signs of tumor lysis syndrome. These are more relevant right after starting treatment, when a lot of cancer cells break down quickly. Symptoms include severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, very little or dark urine, muscle cramps, a fast heartbeat, or confusion. For severe symptoms like trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or anything that feels life-threatening, please call 911 or go to the emergency room. For all the other items we just discussed, including that fever threshold, call your care team right away. Remember, calling is always the right call; no one will think you're overreacting.

script: This treatment might affect your ability to have children, so if this matters to you, please talk to your care team about fertility preservation before you start. You'll need to use effective birth control during your treatment and for some months afterward. Also, it's important not to breastfeed during treatment or for months after your last dose, because chemotherapy drugs can pass into breast milk and harm a nursing infant. Since exact timeframes for both differ by drug, be sure to ask your team for your specific guidance. You should also know that trace amounts of chemo drugs can be present in other bodily fluids during treatment and for some time after. So, to protect your partner, please use a barrier method during intimacy, and again, ask your team for the exact window for this. It's common to notice changes in how you feel about intimacy and your body, and these are absolutely worth talking about with your team. Remember, physical closeness like hugging and holding hands is always safe throughout your treatment.

script: First, it's really important to tell your care team about every medicine, supplement, and vitamin you're taking, because some of these can interact with your treatment. After each infusion, for a certain period—which your team can tell you more about, as it varies by drug—you might have traces of the chemo drugs in your urine, stool, sweat, or vomit. So, while you should use your usual toilet, always remember to close the lid and flush. If you have a low-flow toilet, flush it twice. Also, be sure to wash your hands well afterwards. If there are pregnant household members, please keep them away from contact with any body waste, and always wash any soiled laundry separately.

script: A patient shared that by day 3, when the steroids wear off, they felt completely wiped out. Another patient mentioned a pattern: feeling good the first week on steroids, then having a couple of rough days once they wore off in each cycle. They also found losing their hair gradually, seeing it thin little by little, was harder than shaving it all off; that shaving day was when it truly felt real for them. Someone else experienced nausea and mouth soreness becoming more noticeable with each round, saying brushing their teeth required bracing themselves. They also found the mental fog surprising, noting that some days it took real effort to find the right word or keep a thought straight. Other patients on R-CHOP have shared that the first few days after each infusion tend to be the hardest, but that it often gets more manageable as you settle into the rhythm of cycles. Remember, everyone's experience is different, and your care team is the best judge of what's normal for you.

script: R-CHOP is one of the most established treatments for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. You should know there's a small increased long-term risk of developing a second cancer, like leukemia, after this treatment, and your care team will definitely talk with you more about this. Also, one of the medicines, Doxorubicin, has a lifetime maximum dose because of how it can build up heart risk over time. So, it's really important to tell your team if you've ever received Doxorubicin before, even if it was part of a previous cancer treatment.
